Content:
Suppose we are given the graph of the function [MATH: f(x),] as shown below. The function has critical points at [MATH: x=-1,] [MATH: x=2,] and an inflection point at [MATH: x=0.5.]
How can we sketch the graph of the derivative [MATH: f'(x)?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4a9e6eb093e0376051e68b6f296d2a7e]

Content:
Notice the following:

Content:
- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to [MATH: y=f(x)] is parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis, we have [MATH: f'(x)=0.]
- When [MATH: f(x)] is increasing, we have [MATH: f'(x) > 0.]
- When [MATH: f(x)] is decreasing, we have [MATH: f'(x) < 0.]

Content:
We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: (-\infty,-1)] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: (-1,2)] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: (2,\infty)] |
| [MATH: f] | [MATH: \nearrow] | [MATH: \textrm{max}] | [MATH: \searrow] | [MATH: \textrm{min}] | [MATH: \nearrow] |
| [MATH: f'] | [MATH: +] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: -] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: +] |

Content:
Using this information, we can identify the regions where [MATH: f'(x)] should cross the [MATH: x]-axis. According to the table, these are points [MATH: (-1,0)] and [MATH: (2,0)\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/154ff05101f46cba7912a03db8327859]

Content:
Additionally, we are told that the function has an inflection point at [MATH: x = 0.5.] So [MATH: f''(0.5)=0] and the tangent to the graph of [MATH: y=f'(x)] must be parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis.

Content:
We don't know the exact value of [MATH: f'(0.5)] but from the graph of [MATH: y=f(x),] we can conclude that at [MATH: x = 0.5] the slope is negative. Therefore, we get a point below the [MATH: x]-axis:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d3ecf66501215f33974f353e53ea9e3f]

Content:
Finally, connecting up the parts of the graph above, we get an approximate sketch of [MATH: f'(x)\mathbin{:}]
